page.h1: HTS Chapter 02: Meat and Edible Meat Offal — Export Markets & Foreign Tariffs on U.S. Goods

seo.title: Chapter 02 Export Markets: Tariffs on U.S. Meat by Country
seo.shortDescription: The tariff each top buyer charges on U.S. beef, pork and poultry, with the trade agreement and food-safety regulator for each.

intro: Tariffs are low for most of this chapter. Mexico, Canada, South Korea and Hong Kong charge essentially nothing, and Colombia and the Dominican Republic charge nothing within their quotas. Two buyers cost real money: Japan, where beef still pays about 21% under the U.S.–Japan agreement, and China, which adds 10% to its normal rate on every U.S. good. In every market, the approval that matters most is a food-safety one: the plant must be on the buyer's eligible list and the shipment must carry a USDA FSIS export certificate.
valueBasis: FOB value of U.S. exports, as reported by the United States to UN Comtrade.

0201.rate: About 21% in 2026, falling to 9% by 2033 (U.S.–Japan agreement)

profile.headline: Japan is the one big buyer still charging a real tariff on beef, about 21% this year, falling by about a point a year to 9% in 2033. A volume safeguard can lift it back to 38.5% for a month if U.S. shipments jump. Higher-priced pork cuts pay almost nothing.

profile.headline: China is the market that moved most: purchases fell by half in 2025 to $1.34 billion. Its separate 10–15% tariffs on U.S. pork, beef and chicken were lifted on November 10, 2025, but the extra 10% on every U.S. good remains, and plant registration at China's customs agency decides who can ship at all.

assumptions: Rates come from each market's trade agreement schedule (USMCA, KORUS, U.S.–Japan Trade Agreement, CAFTA-DR, U.S.–Colombia TPA) or its own 2026 customs tariff; Hong Kong has no customs tariff.

One representative subheading stands in for each four-digit group. Rates for China and Japan on the smaller groups (sheep, horse, other meat, fats, salted or dried meat — together under 2% of the chapter) are not individually verified and are marked that way.

China's normal rates are stated as approximate ranges (about 12% on frozen beef and pork, up to about 20% on fresh pork and on chicken cuts and paws) because the exact rate depends on the national tariff line; its extra 10% is added on top.

Dominican Republic and Colombia phase their tariffs out in stages with tariff-rate quotas; the rate shown is the in-quota rate and the direction of travel. Check the exact 2026 stage for a line in the trade.gov FTA Tariff Tool.
National 8–10-digit tariff lines can set a different rate than the six-digit subheading shown here — check the market's own schedule before relying on this page for a transaction.
